subject: physics
question_text: What are the degrees of freedom of a molecule? Give the values for a monoatomic and a diatomic molecule.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 13 Very Short Answer Question 13 (printed p.138). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked against NCERT Class-11 Chapter 13: a monoatomic molecule has 3 degrees of freedom, all translational; a diatomic molecule has 5 at ordinary temperature — 3 translational and 2 rotational — with two further vibrational degrees appearing only at high temperature.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Definition
lines: The degrees of freedom of a
steps.margin_note: First mark. The word independent is what the examiner looks for.
steps.why: A molecule can move along three independent directions, and depending on its shape it can also rotate about independent axes and vibrate along independent bonds — each such independent way of holding energy is one degree of freedom.
common_mistakes: Saying degrees of freedom means the number of atoms in the molecule. It means the number of independent ways to hold energy.

recall.must_convey: That degrees of freedom are the number of independent ways a molecule can hold energy.
accept: independent coordinates needed for its motion
number of independent modes of energy

steps.memory_tip: Each independent way to store energy is one degree of freedom — count the ways, not the atoms.

steps.label: Monoatomic and diatomic values
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both numbers, 3 and 5, are needed; the split into translational and rotational is the extra detail.
steps.why: A monoatomic molecule is a point mass with only three independent directions of motion. A diatomic molecule can also rotate about two axes perpendicular to its bond, giving two more independent ways to hold energy at ordinary temperature.
common_mistakes: Giving 6 degrees of freedom for a diatomic molecule by counting vibration at ordinary temperature, when vibration appears only at high temperature.
Reversing the numbers and writing 5 for monoatomic and 3 for diatomic.

recall.must_convey: That a monoatomic molecule has 3 degrees of freedom and a diatomic molecule has 5 at ordinary temperature, 3 translational and 2 rotational.

steps.memory_tip: Monoatomic: 3, just motion. Diatomic: 5, motion plus 2 rotations about the bond.

insider_note: Give both numbers, 3 and 5 — writing only the definition, with no numbers, earns just the first mark.
